problem: DRL-based indoor navigation needs massive trial-and-error, which is too slow and costly on real robots and hard to reproduce, while existing simulators (AI2-THOR, SUNCG, House3D) use CG scenes with a large visual gap to the real world. Classical indoor navigation also needs pre-installed beacons or pre-built SLAM maps and lacks scene understanding.
motivation: A real-image, interactive, low-cost and reproducible environment would let researchers train and evaluate visual navigation policies with fast virtual actions while still seeing real-world imagery. Without a sim-to-real gap, DRL policies could transfer better to real robots and be compared fairly across labs.
key_idea: Capture a dense grid (20 cm spacing) of real multi-camera images in real rooms with a custom robot, so that a virtual agent can 'walk' between positions and receive real first-person views, and define several DRL navigation tasks on it.
insight: The paper is a dataset and task-formalization paper with no experiments or ablations, so there is no empirical insight. Its core argument is that a discretized grid of real images (positions, 4 directions, stereo pairs) gives an interactive environment without CG rendering artifacts. The action space can be customized per task (e.g. drop turning for a panorama robot, drop lateral moves for a two-wheel robot).
method: Data hierarchy: root > 15 scenes (1-3 rooms each, ~1500 m^2 total) > rooms > thousands of positions per room at 20 cm granularity; each position holds 8 images (front/back/left/right, 2 parallel stereo images each) plus a binary walkable ground-truth map per scene.

Collector robot 'GoodCar': Arduino Mega2560 + two Raspberry Pi 3B, four-track chassis, sonar and code-plate counters, 8 cameras at 1.4 m height; six robots built; scanned in a south-west to north-east lattice pattern.
Moving-control SDK: six discrete actions (MOVE FORWARD/BACKWARD/LEFT/RIGHT by one position = 20 cm, TURN LEFT/RIGHT 90°), subsets chosen per task.
Data processing: cleaning with re-collection of erroneous points, walkable-map building from recorded accessibility, and MC-CNN stereo depth as a pre-computed depth channel.

Target-driven navigation: state = (current image, target image); actions forward/backward/turn; reward large positive at goal plus small negative per step; score from a histogram of steps weighted by max(1-m/10,0) with m collisions; trajectories over 10000 steps are counted as loops.
Multi-target navigation: 2 target images plus current view (3-image state), a smaller separate reward per found target, same metric as target-driven.
Sweeper route planning: actions are the four translational moves with no turning; reward for new positions and penalty for revisits; mAP-like coverage score averaging m/n at new-position steps.
Auto-SLAM: stereo+depth from four directions, reward for newly reconstructed area; evaluated by localization success rate on 10 query images.

setting.backbone: none (dataset paper; ResNet-101 feature extraction and MC-CNN stereo depth mentioned as tools; no trained navigation model reported)
setting.training_data: NavigationNet: 15 real scenes, ~1500 m^2, hundreds of thousands of images captured at 20 cm grid positions
setting.observation: first-person RGB from stereo pairs in 4 directions (8 cameras), optional MC-CNN depth, target image(s) for target tasks
setting.action_space: discrete grid moves: forward/backward/left/right 20 cm and turn left/right 90°
setting.simulator: NavigationNet itself (image-based interactive environment built from real captures)
setting.privileged: none (a ground-truth walkable map is provided with the scenes, needed for Auto-SLAM reward)

numbers_note: No experimental results are reported; the paper only describes the dataset, tasks and metrics (the figures are empty placeholders).
results: No quantitative results are reported. The contribution is a real-image interactive dataset of 15 scenes (~1500 m^2, 20 cm grid, 8 images per position) and four formalized DRL tasks with metrics.
limitations: No baselines or experiments are presented, so the dataset's usefulness and sim-to-real transfer are not validated.
Small scale (15 scenes, ~1500 m^2), with discretized 20 cm positions and 90° turns, and no dynamic elements or object interaction; segmentation labels are left to future work.
Static discrete image grid limits realism of continuous control; the Auto-SLAM and other metrics are only loosely defined.
